alt: A comparison of the Occupiers’ Liability Acts. The 1957 Act protects lawful visitors with the common duty of care, covers property damage and allows limited exclusion; the 1984 Act protects trespassers only when the s1(3) conditions are met, covers injury only, can be discharged by warnings and is silent on exclusion.
caption: Visitor: the 1957 Act. Trespasser: the narrower 1984 Act, for injury only.

alt: Three conditions in s1(3) of the 1984 Act: awareness of the danger, knowledge that the person may be nearby, and a risk that warrants protection. If all three are met, s1(4) imposes a duty of reasonable care against injury. Ratcliff, Tomlinson and Keown failed because the risk was obvious or came from the claimant’s own activity.
caption: Three conditions before any duty; obvious risks and self-created dangers defeat the claim.

alt: Four factors for unreasonable interference: locality (Sturges v Bridgman; St Helen’s Smelting; Coventry v Lawrence), duration and timing (Crown River Cruises; De Keyser’s), sensitivity (Robinson v Kilvert; Network Rail) and malice (Christie v Davey; Hollywood Silver Fox Farm). The parties (Hunter v Canary Wharf; Sedleigh-Denfield; Tetley v Chitty) and defences of prescription and statutory authority follow, with coming to the nuisance and public benefit not defences.
caption: Locality, duration, sensitivity and malice decide whether neighbours must tolerate it.

alt: Five conditions for Rylands v Fletcher: accumulation (Giles v Walker), something likely to do mischief (Transco), non-natural use (Rickards v Lothian; Transco), escape (Read v J Lyons) and damage of a foreseeable type (Cambridge Water). Stannard v Gore failed; the claimant needs an interest in land and cannot claim for personal injury; defences are listed.
caption: All five conditions, an interest in land and no personal injury: a narrow tort.

alt: A cross-section of two plots. A crane jib (Anchor Brewhouse) and an overhanging sign (Kelsen) cross the boundary into the claimant’s airspace, which is protected to a reasonable height (Bernstein v Skyviews); buttresses left on the claimant’s land are a continuing trespass (Holmes v Wilson). Below: trespass is actionable per se, exceeding permission makes a trespasser (The Calgarth), and a continuing trespass gives a fresh cause of action each day.
caption: Any direct crossing of the boundary, on the ground or in the air above it, is a trespass.

alt: A plan of the quarry: a fenced chemical lagoon with a broken section through which Sam and other teenagers enter, and waste seeping under the boundary into the neighbour’s well. Sam claims under the 1984 Act because the s1(3) conditions are met and the duty is breached; the neighbour claims under Rylands v Fletcher, with private nuisance as an alternative.
caption: Status decides the claim: Sam under the 1984 Act; the neighbour under Rylands.
